title: Gin Hangover: Why It Happens, Tonic Sugar, and How to Prevent It
excerpt: Is gin a clean spirit or a hangover trap? What low congeners really mean, whether juniper and botanicals matter, how tonic sugar plays in, and how to avoid a bad gin morning.
metaDescription: Why gin hangovers happen: low congeners, the botanicals myth, tonic sugar and diet mixers, pour sizes, and evidence-based ways to prevent a rough morning.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** gin is one of the cleaner spirits you can drink, but it still gives plenty of people bad hangovers. Gin is made from highly purified neutral spirit, so it carries far fewer congeners (the fermentation by-products that make dark drinks like bourbon and brandy rougher the next day) than most other liquors. The juniper and other botanicals add flavor, not some special hangover chemical. When a gin night goes badly, the usual reasons are simpler: how much you drank, how fast, the sugar in regular tonic and cocktails, poor sleep, and dehydration.

**The quick rules:** Count your drinks, not your mixers, because the amount of alcohol is what matters most. Pour your own measures if you can, since home and bar gin pours are often far bigger than a standard drink. Choose slimline or light tonic, or soda water with lime, if sugary mixers leave you feeling worse. Alternate each gin with a glass of water, eat a real meal beforehand, and stop a couple of hours before bed. If you want to rank gin against everything else on the shelf, see our [least-hangover alcohol ranking](/never-hungover/least-hangover-alcohol-ranked).

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research on hangovers and alcohol. It is not a substitute for a doctor who knows your health history. **See a doctor or get urgent help if** you or someone you're with shows signs of alcohol poisoning (confusion, vomiting while drowsy, slow or irregular breathing, seizures, blue-tinged or very pale skin, or being impossible to wake). In the US, call 911. Talk to a doctor if you regularly get severe hangovers, if your hangovers include heart palpitations or chest pain, or if you take medication that interacts with alcohol. If you're worried about how much you drink, the SAMHSA National Helpline (1-800-662-4357 in the US) is free and confidential.

## Why Gin Gives You a Hangover at All

A hangover is your body dealing with the aftermath of alcohol. Researchers still don't fully agree on every part of the mechanism, but reviews of the science (for example, the work of the Alcohol Hangover Research Group) point to several overlapping causes:

- **Ethanol itself.** The alcohol is the main driver. More alcohol, faster, means worse hangovers. This is true for gin, vodka, whiskey, wine, and beer alike.
- **Acetaldehyde.** Your liver breaks alcohol down into acetaldehyde, a toxic compound, before turning it into harmless acetate. Acetaldehyde is linked to flushing, nausea, and a fast heart rate.
- **Inflammation.** Studies have found raised levels of inflammatory signaling molecules (cytokines) in people with hangovers, which may explain the achy, flu-like feeling.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol helps you fall asleep but breaks up the second half of the night, cutting into deep and REM sleep. You wake up less rested even after a long night in bed. Our guide to [alcohol and REM sleep](/never-hungover/alcohol-and-rem-sleep-complete-scientific-analysis-2025) covers this in detail.
- **Dehydration and the urge to urinate.** Alcohol suppresses a hormone (vasopressin) that tells your kidneys to hold onto water, so you lose more fluid than you take in. Interestingly, studies have found that dehydration doesn't line up neatly with how bad a hangover feels, so it's one factor among several, not the whole story.
- **Congeners.** These are the by-products of fermentation and aging that give drinks their flavor and color. Darker drinks tend to have more, and more congeners are linked to worse hangovers at the same amount of alcohol.

That last point is where gin has a real advantage. The rest of the list applies to gin exactly as much as any other drink.

## The Congener Advantage: What Makes Gin Different

Most gin starts life as a neutral grain spirit, distilled to a very high strength (often around 95% alcohol) in a column still. At that level of purification, most of the congeners that came from fermentation are stripped away. The spirit is then redistilled with juniper and other botanicals, or has botanical extracts added, and diluted to bottling strength. Gin is also usually not aged in barrels, which is where whiskey, brandy, and dark rum pick up a lot of their extra compounds.

The result is a spirit that, chemically, looks much more like vodka than like bourbon. For a deeper look at what congeners are and where they come from, see our explainer on [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol).

### What the research says about clear vs dark spirits

The best-known study here was published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* in 2010 by Rohsenow and colleagues. Young adults drank either bourbon or vodka to a fairly high breath alcohol level on separate nights. On average, people reported worse hangovers after bourbon, which has many times the congener content of vodka. Importantly, next-day performance on tasks like attention and reaction time was impaired after both drinks to a similar degree. In other words, the clearer drink made people *feel* somewhat better, but it didn't spare them the effects of the alcohol itself.

That study didn't test gin directly, but gin and vodka are made in a similar way and both sit at the low end for congeners. Older work, such as a 1973 report by Pawan in the *Proceedings of the Nutrition Society*, ranked drinks by how often they caused hangovers at the same alcohol dose and placed gin and vodka at the gentler end, with brandy and red wine at the harsher end.

So the fair summary is:

- **Gin has fewer congeners than whiskey, brandy, dark rum, or red wine.** That likely makes the average gin hangover a bit milder, drink for drink.
- **The difference is modest compared to the amount you drink.** Five strong gin and tonics will beat two glasses of red wine for a bad morning almost every time.
- **"Clean" is not the same as "safe."** The alcohol still disrupts your sleep, irritates your stomach, and impairs you the next day.

For the matching breakdowns on other spirits, see our guides to [vodka hangovers](/never-hungover/vodka-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide), [whiskey hangovers](/never-hungover/whiskey-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide), and [tequila hangovers](/never-hungover/tequila-hangover-truth).

## The Botanicals Myth-Check: Does Juniper Make Gin Hangovers Worse?

Gin's defining ingredient is juniper, and most gins add others too: coriander seed, angelica root, citrus peel, orris root, cardamom, cassia, and many more. People often blame these botanicals for gin hangovers, or for gin's reputation as a "sad" or "mean" drink. Here's what holds up.

### Myth 1: "Botanicals are congeners, so gin is secretly as bad as dark liquor"

Not really. Botanicals do add aromatic compounds (juniper's main flavor comes from terpenes such as alpha-pinene), but these are present in tiny amounts. They're there to flavor the drink, measured in traces, not in the quantities seen in barrel-aged spirits. There isn't good evidence that the botanical compounds in a normal gin serving make hangovers meaningfully worse. If someone has an allergy or sensitivity to a specific botanical, that's a separate, individual issue.

### Myth 2: "Gin makes you depressed"

This is one of the most persistent drinking myths, and it probably traces back partly to history. In 18th-century London, cheap, often adulterated gin was linked with widespread poverty and social harm (the "Gin Craze"), and the drink earned nicknames like "mother's ruin." That reputation stuck.

There's no good evidence that gin has a unique effect on mood compared to other spirits. Alcohol itself is a depressant of the central nervous system, and the next-day low mood that some people feel (sometimes called "hangxiety") comes from alcohol and poor sleep, not juniper. A 2017 survey published in *BMJ Open* found that people *reported* different emotions with different drinks, with spirits more often linked to feelings like aggression and tearfulness. But that was self-reported association, not proof that the drink causes the feeling. Where, why, and how fast people drink spirits likely explains much of it.

### Myth 3: "Juniper is a diuretic, so gin dehydrates you more"

Juniper has a long history in folk medicine as a diuretic, but the amount in a gin and tonic is tiny. The dehydration you feel after drinking gin comes from the alcohol, the same as with any other drink.

### Myth 4: "Craft or premium gin won't give you a hangover"

A better gin may taste cleaner and may be more pleasant to drink neat, but the ethanol is the same molecule. Premium gin doesn't change how alcohol affects your sleep, your liver, or your stomach. If anything, people sometimes drink nice gin in larger pours because it goes down easily.

## The Tonic Problem: Sugar, Carbonation, and Quinine

For a lot of people, the gin isn't the problem. The tonic is.

### Sugar in regular tonic

Regular tonic water is a sweetened soft drink. Many standard full-sugar tonics carry roughly as much sugar per can as a regular soda, so check the label on the brand you use. A few gin and tonics over an evening can add up to a lot of sugar on top of the alcohol.

Is sugar itself a cause of hangovers? The evidence that sugar directly makes hangovers worse is weak. But sugary mixers can cause problems in more indirect ways:

- **They hide the alcohol.** Sweet, fizzy drinks taste easy, so people tend to drink them faster and lose count.
- **They can upset your stomach** on top of the irritation alcohol already causes.
- **They make it easier to keep going.** A drink that tastes like a soft drink rarely feels like "enough."

If you notice you feel worse after nights on sweet mixers, switching is a reasonable experiment. Light, slimline, or diet tonic, or soda water with a squeeze of lime, cuts the sugar.

### The diet mixer twist

There's a catch with diet mixers. A 2013 study by Marczinski and Stamates in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* found that when people drank vodka mixed with a diet soft drink, their breath alcohol levels came out noticeably higher than when the same vodka was mixed with a sugar-sweetened version. The likely reason is that sugar slows how fast your stomach empties, which slows how quickly alcohol reaches your bloodstream. Without the sugar, alcohol is absorbed faster.

So diet tonic is not a hangover cure. It may cut sugar, but it can also mean you get drunk a bit faster. The fix is to pair the lighter mixer with food and a slower pace, not to treat it as a free pass.

### Carbonation

Bubbles may also speed things up. A 2007 study by Roberts and Robinson in *Alcohol and Alcoholism* found that many people absorbed alcohol faster when it was mixed with carbonated water than when drunk straight or with still water, though not everyone responded the same way. Tonic and soda are both fizzy, so a gin and tonic may hit a little faster than you expect. Again, eating beforehand and slowing down helps.

### Is quinine a problem?

Tonic gets its bitterness from quinine, the same compound once used to treat malaria. In the US, the FDA limits quinine in tonic water to a low level (83 parts per million), far below medical doses. For most people, the quinine in a few tonics isn't a meaningful factor in a hangover.

There are exceptions. Quinine can cause reactions in people who are sensitive to it, and it can interact with certain medications. Anyone who has had a reaction to quinine, or who has been told to avoid it, should skip tonic water. If you take prescription medicine and drink tonic regularly, it's worth a quick question to your pharmacist.

## Gin Cocktails, Ranked From Gentler to Rougher

The same gin can give you very different mornings depending on what it's mixed into. Here's a rough guide based on alcohol content, sugar, and how easy the drink is to overdo. It's general guidance, not a lab ranking.

| Drink | Why it's gentler or rougher |
|---|---|
| Gin and soda with lime | Low sugar, easy to measure, and the long drink slows your pace. Usually the gentlest choice. |
| Gin with light or slimline tonic | Less sugar than regular tonic. Still fizzy, so eat beforehand. |
| Classic gin and tonic | Full-sugar tonic adds a lot of sugar over several rounds and makes drinks go down quickly. |
| Tom Collins or gin fizz | Sweetened with sugar syrup and topped with soda. Pleasant, easy to drink fast. |
| Negroni | Equal parts gin, sweet vermouth, and Campari. Small but strong, and the vermouth and Campari add sugar and extra compounds. |
| Martini (especially large or "dirty") | Mostly straight spirit. A big bar martini can hold two or more standard drinks in one glass. |
| Long Island Iced Tea | Several spirits plus cola and sour mix in one glass. Very strong and sweet, and easy to lose track of. |
| Sloe gin and flavored "pink" gins | Sloe gin is a sweetened liqueur, and many flavored gins add sugar too. Often lower strength but much sweeter. |

The pattern is simple: drinks that are stronger than they taste, or sweet enough to drink quickly, are the ones most likely to cause trouble.

## Gin vs Vodka, Whiskey, and Wine: How Does It Compare?

Since this page completes our spirits series, here's how gin stacks up against the usual suspects.

- **Gin vs vodka.** Very close. Both are made from highly purified neutral spirit and both are low in congeners. Vodka is the most neutral of all, while gin adds trace botanical compounds. In practice, any difference in hangovers between the two is likely to be small compared with how much you drink and what you mix it with.
- **Gin vs whiskey and bourbon.** Gin generally has far fewer congeners. Bourbon in particular is aged in new charred oak barrels and is among the most congener-rich spirits. Drink for drink, gin is likely the gentler choice.
- **Gin vs tequila.** 100% agave blanco tequila is relatively clean, though it carries more congeners than vodka or gin. Cheap "mixto" tequila and aged tequilas (reposado, añejo) carry more.
- **Gin vs rum.** White rum is usually lighter than dark or spiced rum, which can carry more congeners and added sugar.
- **Gin vs red wine.** Red wine contains more congeners, plus compounds like histamine and tannins that some people react to. See our [wine hangover guide](/never-hungover/wine-hangover-guide) for more.

And on the old rhyme about mixing drinks: switching between gin and beer, or gin and wine, isn't harmful in itself. What usually goes wrong on mixed nights is that the total amount of alcohol creeps up. We break that down in [beer before liquor: myth or fact](/never-hungover/beer-before-liquor-myth).

## How Much Gin Is a Standard Drink?

This is where many gin hangovers really start. In the US, one standard drink is about 14 grams of pure alcohol. For gin at 40% alcohol (80 proof), that's a 1.5-ounce (44 ml) pour.

The problem is that many gins are bottled stronger. London Dry gins are often 40% to 47%, and "Navy Strength" gins are around 57%. The stronger the gin, the more alcohol you get in every pour.

And pours vary a lot:

- **Home pours** are notoriously generous. A gin and tonic poured by eye into a large glass can easily hold two standard drinks or more.
- **Large "balloon" glasses**, popular for gin and tonics, make a big pour look small once you add ice and tonic.
- **Martinis and Negronis** are short drinks that can pack two or more standard drinks into one glass.

If you want fewer hangovers from gin, measuring is the most useful single habit. Use a jigger at home, and when you're out, count a martini as two.

## How to Prevent a Gin Hangover

The best tools are not specific to gin. They work because they reduce the amount of alcohol you take in, slow how fast it hits your bloodstream, or protect your sleep. Our full guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) goes deeper, but these are the habits with the most support.

1. **Eat a real meal first.** Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol gets into your blood. This matters even more with fizzy and diet mixers.
2. **Measure your pours.** Use a jigger, choose smaller glasses, and count strong cocktails as more than one drink.
3. **Set a pace.** Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though this varies a lot between people. Drinking faster than that means alcohol builds up.
4. **Alternate with water.** A glass of water between drinks slows you down and helps with fluid loss.
5. **Pick the mixer that works for you.** If sugary drinks leave you worse off, try soda water or light tonic, but keep the pace slow so you don't absorb alcohol faster.
6. **Stop well before bed.** Giving your body a couple of hours to clear some alcohol before sleep can improve sleep quality.
7. **Don't use painkillers "just in case."** Taking acetaminophen (Tylenol) before or while drinking is a bad idea for your liver. See our guide on [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) for the details.

### Where supplements fit (and where they don't)

Some people add a supplement to their routine. It's worth being clear about what the evidence does and doesn't show.

**DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree. A well-known 2012 study by Shen and colleagues in the *Journal of Neuroscience* found that DHM reduced signs of alcohol intoxication and withdrawal in rats, and other animal and lab studies suggest it may support alcohol metabolism and the liver. Human data are much more limited, and there are no large clinical trials showing that DHM prevents hangovers. It's a reasonable thing to try if you're curious, but it is not a substitute for drinking less, and it does not make it safe to drink more or to drive.

If you want to try DHM, two widely used options are [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the lower-cost [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands side by side. Talk to your doctor before adding any supplement if you take prescription medication or have liver disease.

For a broader look at what to take and when, see [what to take before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-take-before-drinking).

## How to Feel Better the Morning After Gin

Nothing reliably cures a hangover except time. But some things can make the morning easier:

- **Drink water steadily.** Small, regular amounts are easier on an upset stomach than a big glass all at once. An oral rehydration drink can help if you were sick. Our roundup of [hangover recovery drinks](/never-hungover/best-hangover-recovery-drinks) compares the options.
- **Eat something simple.** Toast, crackers, eggs, rice, or bananas are easy on the stomach and help steady your blood sugar.
- **Be careful with painkillers.** If you need one, read the label, take a single standard dose with food, and don't combine it with more alcohol. Ibuprofen and other NSAIDs can irritate an already irritated stomach, and acetaminophen adds work for the liver after heavy drinking.
- **Skip "hair of the dog."** Another gin and tonic may delay symptoms, but it just pushes the hangover later and adds more alcohol for your body to clear.
- **Rest.** Since poor sleep is a big part of how hangovers feel, a nap or an early night often helps more than anything else.

If your hangover lasts well into a second day, that's usually a sign of a very heavy night, poor sleep, or dehydration. Our guide to the [two-day hangover](/never-hungover/two-day-hangover) explains why it happens and when to see a doctor.

### When it's more than a hangover

Get medical help if someone can't be woken, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has a seizure, keeps vomiting and can't keep fluids down, or seems confused long after drinking. These can be signs of alcohol poisoning, which is an emergency. In the US, call 911. Don't leave the person alone, and if they're lying down, roll them onto their side.

## Who Should Be Extra Careful With Gin

Gin's clean reputation can make it feel harmless. These groups should be more careful with any alcohol, gin included:

- **People taking medications that interact with alcohol**, such as sedatives, sleep aids, some antidepressants, some antibiotics, and blood thinners. Ask a pharmacist if you're not sure.
- **People with liver disease, heart rhythm problems, or diabetes.** Sugary tonic and cocktails can also affect blood sugar.
- **Anyone who has reacted to quinine** should avoid tonic water.
- **People who are pregnant or trying to get pregnant.** No amount of alcohol is known to be safe during pregnancy.
- **Anyone who finds that hangovers are becoming frequent or severe.** That can be a sign it's time to look at how much and how often you drink, and a doctor can help without judgment.

## The Bottom Line

- **Gin is a low-congener spirit**, much like vodka, so drink for drink it tends to cause milder hangovers than whiskey, brandy, dark rum, or red wine.
- **The botanicals are not the problem.** Juniper and other botanicals are present in trace amounts, and there's no good evidence they make hangovers worse or that gin uniquely causes low mood.
- **Tonic matters.** Regular tonic adds a lot of sugar and makes drinks easy to overdo. Diet and fizzy mixers may speed up alcohol absorption, so pair them with food and a slower pace.
- **Pour size matters most.** Strong gins, big glasses, and short cocktails like martinis can hide two or more standard drinks.
- **No spirit or supplement cancels out drinking too much.** Eating first, measuring, pacing, and stopping before bed do more than anything you can buy.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does gin give you a worse hangover than other alcohol?**

Usually not. Gin is made from highly purified neutral spirit and is low in congeners, the by-products linked to worse hangovers in drinks like bourbon, brandy, and red wine. Drink for drink, gin tends to fall at the gentler end, close to vodka. The amount of alcohol you drink, the sugar in your mixers, and how well you sleep matter far more than the choice of gin over another spirit.

**Is gin or vodka better for avoiding a hangover?**

They're very similar. Both are low-congener spirits made from neutral spirit. Vodka is the most neutral, while gin adds small amounts of botanical flavor compounds. Any difference in hangovers between them is likely small compared to how much you drink, how fast, and what you mix it with.

**Does tonic water make a gin hangover worse?**

It can contribute. Regular tonic is a sugar-sweetened soft drink, and its sweetness makes gin easy to drink quickly. The evidence that sugar directly causes hangovers is weak, but sweet mixers can lead to drinking more and upsetting your stomach. Diet tonic cuts sugar but may let alcohol be absorbed a bit faster, so eat first and keep a steady pace either way.

**Do the botanicals in gin cause hangovers?**

There's no good evidence that they do. Juniper and other botanicals are present in trace amounts for flavor. They're not the same as the heavy congener load in barrel-aged spirits. If you react to a specific botanical, that's an individual sensitivity, not a general rule.

**Does gin make you sad or depressed?**

There's no good evidence that gin affects mood differently from other spirits. Its reputation as "mother's ruin" comes largely from 18th-century London history. Alcohol itself is a depressant, and next-day anxiety or low mood is linked to alcohol and poor sleep, not to juniper.

**Is the quinine in tonic water safe with alcohol?**

For most people, yes. Tonic water contains only a small amount of quinine, far below medical doses, and the FDA caps it at a low level in the US. People who have reacted to quinine before, or who take medications that might interact with it, should avoid tonic water and ask a pharmacist if unsure.

**How many gin and tonics before a hangover?**

There's no safe number that applies to everyone, because body size, food, sleep, pace, and genetics all play a role. As a rough guide, one standard drink is 1.5 ounces (44 ml) of 40% gin, and many home and bar gin and tonics contain more than that. Keeping to one measured drink per hour, with food and water, makes a hangover much less likely.

**Can DHM prevent a gin hangover?**

DHM has promising results in animal and lab studies, but human evidence is limited, and there's no strong proof that it prevents hangovers. Some people find it helpful as part of a routine that includes eating, pacing, and water. It doesn't make it safe to drink more or to drive. Check with your doctor first if you take medication or have liver disease.
